newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysian prince details children's return in book.
newsitem.headline: Malaysian prince details children's return in book.

text.p: A Malaysian prince who staged a dramatic mission four years ago to take back his two children from his Australian ex-wife is telling his side of the story in a just-published book.
Raja Kamarul Bahrin Shah, a nephew of the Sultan of Malaysia's northeastern Terengganu state, unveiled "The Raja Bahrin Story" at a news conference on Thursday.
His account, written with mission co-plotter Australian Bryan Wickham, follows a book by ex-wife Jacqueline Gillespie titled "Once I was a Princess" last year.
The 41-year-old architect said the 273-page book is his attempt to counter what he believes is biased Australian media coverage.

"We need to have the record set straight," he said. "I hope this book does get to Australia." He also criticised Australian family courts at the news conference, accusing them of being anti-Asian and anti-Moslem.
Gillespie was 17 when she married Raja Kamarul in 1981. They had met while he was studying at Melbourne University.
Four years later, they separated, and Raja Kamarul accused Gillespie of kidnapping their son and daughter when she took them to Australia for a visit.

In 1992, after seven years of fighting for custody of the children, who had been awarded to his wife by an Australian court, Raja Kamarul grabbed the children during an access visit. His son, Iddin, was then aged 10, and the daughter, Shah, eight.
In a journey that covered thousands of kilometres across Australia and the Indonesian archipelago by road, sea and air, the Malaysian prince and Wickham took the children back to Malaysia.
The burly Wickham, 59, a Perth resident, who works in construction, became friends with the soft-spoken, slightly-built Raja Kamarul during a chance encounter in 1988 at Singapore's Changi Airport.
Wickham, who spent two of his six years in the Australian Regular Army in Malaysia, was jailed for several months in Australia for his role in the plot.
"I wrote part of it (the book) in jail to help pass the time," Wickham told reporters. "Raja got a raw deal from the Australian courts. I believe I didn't break the law, I righted a wrong."
Malaysia has rejected an Australian request to extradite Raja Kamarul.
Raja Kamarul said he has read parts of Gillespie's book, and said allegations of spousal abuse made in the book about him are false.
Gillespie's book is banned in Malaysia. Raja Kamarul said he had nothing to do with that decision, adding he has no royal privileges, and did not use political connections to aid his custody battle.
Gillespie could not be reached for comment.
The children's mother has not given up the fight, and has sought help from Australian leaders. They have declined, saying it is a personal matter and should be left to the law.
Raja Kamarul said he would permit Gillespie to see Iddin, now 13 and Shah, 11, in a supervised visit. But he said she has not requested to see them.
"She writes them maybe twice a year and the children feel, I suppose, some form of abandonment," he said.
